title: How Far Back Does a Background Check Go? The 7-Year Rule by State
description: How far back does a background check go? Arrests usually drop off after 7 years, but convictions can stay. See federal rules, state limits and how to dispute.
lede: Maybe you have an arrest from years ago, or a conviction you've worked hard to put behind you. Now there's a job offer, an apartment or a license on the line, and one question keeps coming back: how far back will they look?

The honest answer is that it depends. It depends on what kind of record it is, who is running the check, what the job pays, and which state you live in. An old arrest that never led to a conviction is treated very differently from a conviction.

The good news is that there are real limits. Federal law keeps most old arrests off commercial background checks after seven years, and several states go further. Records that were expunged or sealed should not show up at all.

This guide explains the federal seven-year rule in plain words, lists the states with stricter limits, explains how FBI fingerprint checks differ, and walks through what to do if something old or cleared shows up on your report.
takeaways: Under federal law, background check companies generally can't report arrests that didn't lead to a conviction once they are more than seven years old.
Federal law sets no time limit for reporting convictions. Some states do, usually seven years.
The federal seven-year limit doesn't apply to jobs paying $75,000 a year or more.
FBI and state fingerprint checks, often used for licenses and some jobs, work under different rules than commercial background checks.
Expunged and sealed records should not appear on a background check. If one does, you can dispute it for free, and the company generally has 30 days to investigate.

sections.heading: How Far Back Does a Background Check Go Under Federal Law?
paragraphs: Most employers and landlords buy background checks from private companies. Federal law calls these companies consumer reporting agencies, and the Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA) sets limits on what they can report.

The key rule is in 15 U.S.C. 1681c. It says no consumer reporting agency may report "Civil suits, civil judgments, and records of arrest that, from date of entry, antedate the report by more than seven years or until the governing statute of limitations has expired, whichever is the longer period."
The same section also bars "Any other adverse item of information, other than records of convictions of crimes which antedates the report by more than seven years."

Put simply: arrests and other negative items generally drop off after seven years. Convictions are the exception. The CFPB puts it this way: "There is no federal time limit for how long criminal convictions can stay on your report, although some states may have different rules."

sections.heading: Can a Background Check Show Convictions Older Than 7 Years?
paragraphs: Yes, under federal law. Convictions were not always treated this way. Until 1998, the FCRA also limited convictions to seven years. That year, Congress added the words "other than records of convictions of crimes" to the law, which removed convictions from the seven-year limit.

Arrests that did not lead to a conviction are different. For arrests, the federal clock runs seven years "from date of entry." In a 2024 advisory opinion, the CFPB said some companies had wrongly started the clock on dismissed cases at the dismissal date instead, which kept them on reports too long. It said a dismissed charge "cannot be reported beyond the seven-year period that begins to run at the time of the charge."
The CFPB withdrew that advisory opinion in May 2025, saying the withdrawal "is not necessarily final." The statute's own words, "from date of entry," have not changed.
Several states limit convictions too. We cover those below.

sections.heading: What Is the $75,000 Salary Exception?
paragraphs: The seven-year limit has exceptions. Under 15 U.S.C. 1681c(b), it does not apply to a report used for "the employment of any individual at an annual salary which equals, or which may reasonably be expected to equal $75,000, or more."
The federal seven-year limit does not apply to jobs paying $75,000 a year or more.

The same goes for credit of $150,000 or more and life insurance of $150,000 or more. So for a job at that pay level, a background check company may report arrests older than seven years under federal law. State law may still limit it, depending on the state.

sections.heading: Which States Limit How Far Back a Background Check Can Go?
paragraphs: Some states have their own laws for background check companies, and several are stricter than federal law. The biggest difference: in the states below, convictions are also limited to seven years, usually counted from the date of disposition, release or parole rather than from the arrest.
Many of these states have their own salary exception, and it is often much lower than the federal $75,000. A few have none for jobs at all.

One caution. Federal law lets state rules on this subject stand only if the state law was in effect on September 30, 1996. Whether a given state's rule, or a later change to it, still applies is a legal question. A lawyer can tell you how it works in your state.
Here are the ten states we checked. Other states may have rules we did not review.

sections.heading: Do FBI Fingerprint Background Checks Have a Time Limit?
paragraphs: An FBI or state fingerprint check is a different thing from a commercial background check. It comes from government records built from fingerprints, not from a private company's database. It is used for some licenses and jobs, when a law allows it.

Under federal rules, the FBI shares records with state and local governments "for purposes of employment and licensing" when a state law authorizes it, and with banks and some other industries. The rule (28 CFR 50.12) says the FBI "has made all data on identification records available for such purposes." The seven-year limit in the FCRA is written for consumer reporting agencies, and the FBI rule we read does not contain one. So expect a fingerprint check to show your whole record, including old arrests.

There is a protection. Officials who use an FBI record for a license or job "shall provide the applicants the opportunity to complete, or challenge the accuracy of, the information contained in the FBI identification record." They should not deny you until you have had a reasonable time to correct the record, or have declined to.

Because a fingerprint check can reach back further, it helps to see your own record first. Our guide /guides/how-to-get-a-copy-of-your-criminal-record explains how to request your FBI and state records.

sections.heading: Is a Background Check Different for a Job, an Apartment or a License?
paragraphs: For jobs and apartments, the same federal seven-year rule applies when the check comes from a background check company. The FTC says tenant screening companies "generally cannot report negative information if it's older than seven years," but "there is no time limit for criminal convictions."

Jobs: an employer must tell you in writing, in a separate document, and get your written permission before ordering a check. Before turning you down because of the report, it must give you a copy and a summary of your rights. Higher-paying jobs may fall under the $75,000 exception.

Apartments: tenant reports can include "criminal records, including arrest, charge, and conviction records," plus eviction and credit history. If a landlord turns you down, charges more rent or asks for a bigger deposit because of the report, it must give you a notice naming the company.
Licenses: licensing agencies may use FBI fingerprint checks when a state law authorizes it, and the FBI rule we read sets no seven-year limit. Licensing rules vary by state and by profession.

sections.heading: What Are Ban-the-Box and Fair Chance Laws?
paragraphs: These laws don't change how far back a check goes. They change when an employer can ask. The FTC notes that "Laws in your city or state might impact if or when employers can ask about your criminal or credit history."
For federal jobs, 5 U.S.C. 9202 bars agencies from asking about criminal history before a conditional job offer, with some exceptions.

California is one state example. Its Fair Chance Act covers employers with five or more employees. They can't ask about convictions before a conditional offer, and they can't consider arrests that didn't lead to a conviction, diversion, or convictions that were sealed, dismissed or expunged. If an employer leans toward saying no, it must do an individualized assessment and give you at least five business days to respond. Rules elsewhere vary, so check your state and city.

sections.heading: Can Expunged or Sealed Records Show Up on a Background Check?
paragraphs: They shouldn't. The CFPB tells consumers: "If any of your criminal records was expunged or removed from public records, they should not appear on your report." The FTC lists "criminal record or eviction information that was sealed or expunged" as a common error.
Expunged and sealed records should not appear on a commercial background check.

The legal hook is the FCRA's accuracy rule. Companies must "follow reasonable procedures to assure maximum possible accuracy." In 2024 the CFPB said that means having procedures to avoid reporting records that were "expunged, sealed, or otherwise legally restricted from public access." That opinion was withdrawn in May 2025, though the accuracy rule itself is unchanged and the CFPB and FTC consumer pages still say these records should not appear. Some states also spell it out. Colorado's law, for example, bars reporting "Sealed records, expunged records, and records that did not result in a conviction."
Still, mistakes happen. Our guide /guides/expunged-record-showing-on-background-check explains why and what to do.

sections.heading: How Do I Dispute an Old or Expunged Record on a Background Check?
paragraphs: If a report shows an arrest older than seven years, a record that was expunged or sealed, or anything that isn't accurate, you can dispute it. It's free.

Under 15 U.S.C. 1681i, the company must, "free of charge, conduct a reasonable reinvestigation" and fix or delete the item within 30 days of getting your dispute. It can take up to 15 more days if you send new information during those 30 days.
If the company doesn't fix it, you can submit a complaint to the CFPB or report it to the FTC. If your rights were violated, you may be able to bring a lawsuit.
bullets: Get the report. If you were turned down, you can get a free copy from the company if you ask within 60 days of the notice.
Mark each item that is too old, was expunged or sealed, or isn't yours.
Write to the background check company. Describe the error and include copies, not originals, of your court papers, such as an expungement order.
Contact whoever supplied the wrong information too. For criminal records, you can also contact the court.
When the company answers, check the corrected report and ask it to send a copy to the employer or landlord.

next_steps: Check your own record first. Request your FBI and state records so you know what a fingerprint check will show. See /guides/how-to-get-a-copy-of-your-criminal-record.
Look up your state's rules. Your state may limit convictions to seven years or set its own salary exception. Start at /states.
Dispute anything too old or cleared. Write to the background check company with copies of your court papers, and contact the court if its records are wrong.
Think about clearing what's left. Expunged and sealed records should not appear on commercial checks. Find a record-clearing lawyer in your city at /cities.
Get free help if you need it. Legal aid groups can help with disputes and record clearing. See /free-expungement-help.
